content: Ungulates, which are mammals characterized by their hooves, are a diverse group of animals that primarily use the tips of their toes to support their body weight during locomotion. These mammals are classified into several orders, with six to eight of these orders still existing today. However, there is ongoing debate among scientists regarding whether ungulates form a clade (a group based on evolutionary relationships) or are simply a phenetic group (a group based on shared physical traits without necessarily being closely related). This debate arises because not all ungulates appear to be as closely related as previously thought. Historically, ungulates were considered a single order, but they have since been divided into several distinct orders, including Perissodactyla (odd-toed ungulates), Artiodactyla (even-toed ungulates), Tubulidentata, Hyracoidea, Sirenia, and Proboscidea. Members of Perissodactyla, Artiodactyla, and Cetacea (whales and dolphins) are often referred to as true ungulates, while members of Proboscidea (elephants), Sirenia (manatees and dugongs), Hyracoidea (hyraxes), and Tubulidentata (aardvarks) are classified as subungulates or Paenungulata. Examples of modern ungulates include horses, zebras, donkeys, cattle, bison, rhinoceroses, camels, hippopotamuses, goats, pigs, sheep, giraffes, okapis, deer, tapirs, antelopes, and gazelles. The largest groups of ungulates are the Perissodactyla and Artiodactyla, which also represent the majority of large terrestrial mammals. These two groups first appeared during the late Paleocene and early Eocene epochs, approximately 54 million years ago, and have since diversified into a wide range of species across multiple continents. Interestingly, while whales and dolphins lack many of the typical morphological traits of ungulates, recent evidence suggests that they are descended from early artiodactyls, making them closely related to even-toed ungulates such as cattle and hippopotamuses. This discovery has led to the proposal of a new order, Cetartiodactyla, which combines Artiodactyla and Cetacea to reflect their shared ancestry. However, some researchers argue that it is sufficient to classify Cetacea as a subgroup within Artiodactyla. The orders Hyracoidea, Sirenia, and Proboscidea are collectively known as Paenungulata, while Tubulidentata is also considered part of the ungulate group. Additionally, Macroscelidea (elephant shrews) have been interpreted as ungulates based on dental and genetic evidence. Some studies link Tubulidentata with Paenungulata under the group Pseudoungulata. However, genetic studies indicate that these animals are not closely related to artiodactyls and perissodactyls. Instead, their closest relatives are Afrotheria, a superorder that includes Pseudoungulata and Afrosoricida (tenrecs and golden moles). Fossil evidence reveals that extinct ungulate groups include embritopods, desmostylians, mesonychids, condylarths, and various South American and Paleogene lineages. Most ungulates exhibit certain shared traits, such as reduced canine teeth, bunodont molars (molars with low, rounded cusps), and a specialized ankle bone called the astragalus with a short, robust head. Another notable characteristic is the fusion of the radius and ulna in the forelimbs, which prevents rotation of the forelimb. This skeletal adaptation is present in most modern ungulates but was absent in early ungulates like arctocyonids. The fusion of these bones is considered a homologous trait inherited from a common ancestor. Ungulates diversified rapidly during the Eocene epoch but are believed to have originated as far back as the late Cretaceous period. While most ungulates are herbivorous, some, such as mesonychians and whales, are omnivorous or even predatory. The evolutionary history of ungulates is complex, with their characteristic morphology appearing independently in three separate lineages: Meridiungulata (South American ungulates), Afrotheria, and the true ungulates within Laurasiatheria. This phenomenon is an example of convergent evolution, where similar traits evolve independently in unrelated groups. Recent molecular phylogenetic studies have challenged traditional views of ungulate relationships. These studies suggest that Perissodactyla and Cetartiodactyla are more closely related to Carnivora (carnivores) and Pholidota (pangolins) than to Pseudoungulata. Additionally, extinct South American ungulates, which evolved in isolation during the mid-to-late Paleocene, are grouped under the superorder Meridiungulata. Some researchers believe these animals are unrelated to other ungulates and instead share closer ties with Afrotheria and Xenarthra (armadillos, sloths, and anteaters) within the supercohort Atlantogenata. The position of other extinct ungulates, such as embritopods and desmostylians, remains unclear. These groups are often considered relatives of Paenungulata and members of Afrotheria. Meanwhile, condylarths, once thought to be the ancestors of all ungulates, are now regarded as part of the cohort Laurasiatheria. As a result, only Perissodactyla and Artiodactyla are believed to have descended from condylarths, assuming that the animals historically grouped under Condylarthra are even related to one another. In summary, the typical ungulate morphology appears to have evolved independently in multiple lineages, highlighting the complexity of their evolutionary history. This conclusion is met with skepticism by some scientists, who argue that there is insufficient morphological evidence to divide ungulates into so many unrelated clades.
